rationale: This sample is effectively a 191-byte, 3-function binary (main plus init/start stubs) whose real work is a single printf, so absolute runtime and size budgets are huge relative to baseline and aggressive obfuscation is cheap in absolute terms; accordingly SUB gets the highest security/diversity weights and near-max tolerance for cost and risk since instruction substitution is semantically safe and effective on arithmetic-free code paths as a cheap baseline transform, BCF and FLA follow closely because bogus control flow and flattening deliver the strongest reverse-engineering resistance on a tiny CFG where a single basic block dominates and can be flattened with negligible absolute overhead, and SPLIT is kept as a low-cost amplifier of FLA/BCF with maximal cost tolerance. IBR is weighted for solid security and diversity but with reduced RuntimeCost/SizeCost tolerance because opaque-block insertion inflates text size multiplicatively and the sample's 191-byte text would balloon visibly, which matters for anything other than absolute overhead; ICALL is included at moderate weights with the lowest CorrectnessRisk tolerance since indirect-call transformation on a hello-style main with no indirect call sites offers little benefit and risks calling-convention breakage; and IGV is effectively disabled (lowest weights across all dimensions) because a global-variable-hiding pass needs meaningful global state and multi-function data flow that this 3-function binary does not have. CorrectnessRisk tolerances are kept high for the provably-safe transforms (SUB, SPLIT) and low for the structurally invasive ones (ICALL, IGV) so the selector favors safe passes for the tiny, correctness-critical main while still allowing BCF/FLA to apply where their features favor them.
